## A Resolution in Honor of Beverly's 2026 Senior of the Year

*presented by the Beverly City Council*
*with great appreciation for the volunteerism, community-mindedness, and caring*
*of our esteemed honoree*

Whereas Gail Dionne, a long-time part of the Beverly community for more than fifty years and a resident of the City's wonderful Ward 3, has been named this year's Beverly Senior of the Year;

Whereas Gail moved from Salem, MA to the City of Beverly with her late husband John to put down roots, to nurture and raise their family, and to become fully and generously a part of the community;

Whereas Gail was a dedicated part of the Beverly Public Schools team for many years, forging strong relationships with students and their families, as well as with her colleagues;

Whereas Gail and John shared a love of being on the water and, especially, of sailing, spending years as beloved members of Salem's Palmer Cove Yacht Club and loving times when they could feel the thrill of the wind in the sails and having the boat heeled over well, whether on a casual sail, or when on a beat, a reach, or a run to make the next mark in a sailboat race;

Whereas Gail is extremely generous with her time and with her deeply caring heart, and is always the first one to step up to offer help when someone needs a ride to an appointment or to the grocery store, or when someone simply needs a caring and listening ear or an invitation and encouragement to attend an event or activity at the Beverly Senior Center in a time of feeling alone or isolated;

Whereas Gail is an active and engaged member of the Beverly Senior Center community – a joyful regular part the bocce team, leader of the exercise class, active participant in walking club and in the Mah Jong group, helper in the kitchen, ready hand to help serve up the pizza for a fun-filled movie night, and an overall dedicated volunteer and welcoming face for the many activities and events that offer so many connections to and for others at the Senior Center;

Whereas Gail, with her generous spirit and caring heart, embodies in every way the idea of generous volunteer leadership; Gail is always ready to help when and where she is needed, helping to build and strengthen a sense of community and communal care as she does so, while giving with her whole heart for its own sake, without expectation of recognition or anything in return; and

Whereas Gail truly exhibits the community pride and caring, the sense of leadership, and joy in sharing kindness and giving of herself in service to others that embodies true volunteerism and generosity of spirit;

*NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED* that the Beverly City Council does hereby congratulate, thank, and honor Beverly's 2026 Senior of the Year, Gail Dionne, and wishes her much happiness, success, and good health, and orders that the City Clerk spread a copy of this Resolution upon the City Records.

**Be it ordained by the City Council of the City of Beverly as follows:**

City Ordinance Chapter 300 is amended by inserting a new section to be titled Section 300-142 "Temporary Moratorium on construction of Data Centers until November 30, 2027" the purpose of which is to adopt a temporary moratorium on the use, construction, development, expansion, or conversion of land or structures for Data Centers. The new section shall read as follows:

**Article XVII**

**Section 300-142**

Temporary Moratorium on construction of Data Centers until November 30, 2027.

**1. Purpose.**

The purpose of this temporary moratorium is to provide the City an opportunity to better understand the impacts, if any, that the construction, expansion, and operation of Data Centers (defined below) will have on the City of Beverly. As a result, the City shall analyze and study the impacts of said construction on public safety, the school district, electrical demand, water, sewer, and roadway infrastructures, noise, environmental resources and the overall community character.

Currently, Chapter 300 of the City's General Code (the City's Zoning Ordinances) does not identify Data Center as a permitted use, nor are there specific restrictions on such use. The regulation of Data Centers raises novel and complex legal, planning, and infrastructure issues or concerns. The City needs time to study, consider, and engage in decision-making regarding this new use and the potential impacts of the use and to undertake a planning process to develop appropriate and reasonable regulations for Data Centers, consistent with M.G.L. c. 40A.

The City hereby adopts a temporary moratorium, effective immediately, on the use of land and structures and any new construction and development in the City of Beverly for Data Centers in order to allow the City sufficient time to engage in a planning process to address the effects of such structures and uses in the City and to adopt provisions of the Zoning Ordinances in a manner consistent with sound land use planning goals and objectives.

**2. Moratorium.**

The City of Beverly hereby adopts a temporary moratorium on the use, construction, development, expansion, or conversion of land or structures for Data Centers. During the moratorium period, the City shall not accept, process, or approve any application for a Data Center, including but not limited to:

- Building permits;
- Special permits;
- Site plan approval;
- Any other zoning or land use approvals.

**3. Definitions.**

DATA CENTER(S): a building or group of buildings, the primary use of which is to house computer systems, servers, data storage equipment, networking equipment, and associated infrastructure necessary for the processing, storage, and distribution of data and digital applications.

**4. Intent.**

For the reasons set forth in the purpose Sections above, and notwithstanding any other provision of the Zoning Ordinance to the contrary, the City hereby adopts a moratorium on the use of any land or structure for Data Centers in all zoning districts in the City. The moratorium shall be in effect until such time that the City Council enacts a Zoning Ordinance specifically addressing Data Centers in the City of Beverly or through November 30, 2027, which date is sooner. During the moratorium period, the City shall undertake a planning process to evaluate the potential impacts of Data Centers and related uses in the City, consider public health and safety implications, if any, of Data Centers, consider the appropriate locations within the City, if any, for Data Centers, review and consider State regulations and case law, and develop and enact new Zoning Ordinances to address these issues, including the use of any land or structures therefore.

**5. Severability.**

The provisions of this ordinance are severable. If any provision, paragraph, sentence, or clause of this ordinance or the application thereof to any person, establishment, or circumstances shall be held invalid, such invalidity shall not affect the other provisions or application of this ordinance.

An Ordinance Amending Chapter [X], Section [Y] of the Ordinances of the City of Beverly Regarding Executive Administration Out-of-State Travel and Expenditure of Public Funds.

Be it ordained by the City Council of the City of Beverly as follows:

## Section 1. Purpose and Intent

The purpose of this ordinance is to establish strict fiscal accountability, oversight, and transparency regarding out-of-state travel by the executive administration. This ensures that all travel paid for by municipal funds serves an essential public purpose with a clear and defined benefit to the City of Beverly.

## Section 2. Definitions

- "Administration" or "Executive Administration": Shall mean the Mayor, their direct appointees, department heads, and all employees operating under the authority of the executive branch.
- "Out-of-State Travel": Travel to destinations outside the geographical boundaries of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts.
- "Public Funds": Any monies appropriated by the City Council, including local tax revenues, municipal grants, or revolving funds.

## Section 3. Prior Approval Required for Out-of-State Travel

1. City Council Authorization: No public funds shall be expended, nor shall any member of the Executive Administration be reimbursed, for out-of-state travel unless such travel has been approved by a majority vote of the City Council at a regularly scheduled meeting.
2. Submission Timeline: A formal written request for out-of-state travel must be submitted to the City Clerk for inclusion on the City Council agenda no less than fourteen (14) business days prior to the scheduled departure.

## Section 4. Content of Travel Request

Any request for out-of-state travel submitted by the Administration must include a completed Travel Authorization Form detailed with:

1. The name and title of the municipal employee(s) traveling.
2. The destination, dates of travel, and the specific event, conference, or municipal business being conducted.
3. An itemized estimate of all associated costs, including transportation, lodging, registration fees, and meals.
4. A written justification detailing the direct benefit of the travel to the operations of the City of Beverly.
5. The specific municipal account and line-item from which the travel will be funded.

## Section 5. Limitations on Travel and Reimbursements

1. Funding Source Restrictions: In accordance with M.G.L. c. 268A, no member of the Administration shall accept direct vendor-paid travel or accommodation subsidies unless expressly authorized by a specific local ordinance regulating vendor payments or accepted as a formal grant under M.G.L. c. 44, § 53.
2. Statutory Exclusions: In accordance with M.G.L. c. 44, § 58, no city funds shall be expended or reimbursed for wines, liquors, or cigars incurred during any travel status.
3. Frequency Cap: No individual member of the Administration shall be authorized for more than two (2) out-of-state travel events per fiscal year, unless mandated by an active employment contract or collective bargaining agreement.

## Section 6. Post-Travel Reporting

Within thirty (30) days of returning from authorized out-of-state travel, the traveling administrator must submit a summary report to the City Council detailing the findings, certifications, or direct municipal benefits obtained during the trip, alongside itemized receipts filed with the City Auditor.

## Section 7. Emergency Exemptions

The provisions of Section 3 may be waived only in the event of a public safety emergency or time-sensitive legal proceeding affecting the City. In such instances, the Mayor must provide a written notification and fiscal breakdown of the emergency travel to the City Council within forty-eight (48) hours of the departure.

## Section 8. Enforcement and Penalty

Any expenditure of public funds for out-of-state travel that violates this ordinance shall be considered an unauthorized expenditure. The individual who incurred the cost will not be reimbursed, and any unauthorized corporate card charges or advances must be repaid to the City treasury within ten (10) business days.

## Section 9. Severability

The provisions of this ordinance are severable. If any provision is declared unconstitutional or invalid, the remaining provisions shall remain in full force and effect.

## Section 10. Effective Date

This ordinance shall take effect upon passage.

### Kestrel, mayor at odds on creating nature learning center at Camp Paradise

By Michael McHugh | Staff Writer
Jan 9, 2026

1 of 3

*Jessica Kagle of Kestrel Educational Adventures is proposing a nature learning center at Camp Paradise, a 12-acre property off Col Street that was bought by the city of Beverly in 2015.*
By Michael McHugh/Staff Writer

BEVERLY — A natural science education organization and community members are pushing for the creation of a nature learning center at Camp Paradise in Beverly, but the city claims that legal restrictions on use of the land would make the proposed use infeasible.

Camp Paradise is a 12-acre property on Cole Street that was bought by the city in 2013 for $950,000 from Girl Scouts of Eastern Massachusetts through a combination of community preservation money, state grants, and the Beverly Park and Recreation Department's budget.

Although the property had been appraised to be able to accommodate residential and commercial development, the original acquisition document dictates the land will remain for the purposes of "conservation, scientific study, and nature recreation."

In addition to a 1,000-square-foot recreation building, the site includes a red maple swamp, woodlands, a pond, and a couple of vernal pools — with the intersecting environments creating a high level of biodiversity for such a small property.

Kestrel Educational Adventures, a nature science education organization that frequently utilizes and rents out the space, has a "conservation club" program designed for students aged 10-16. The conservation club has conducted a service project to explore the ponds and collect data to submit to the state and the city's own conservation staff, to aid in the understanding and protection of the sensitive breeding wildlife onsite.

Through its study of local wildlife through trail cams and direct observation, the club has found evidence of wood frogs, spotted salamanders, eastern newts, various dragonflies and damselflies, deer, bobcats, snapping turtles, and a variety of other wildlife.

"I love getting to consistently explore the waters there," said Alyssa Magill, a Beverly High School freshman who has been in the conservation club for four years. "There's a variety of different life within it, and it was fun to go in with nets and see everything that came up. I hadn't experienced anything like that before going to Camp Paradise.

"It's definitely a very different experience getting into the water to see this wildlife for yourself, instead of just hearing about it or seeing pictures."

The camp's wide range of amphibians, invertebrates, and other animals have been documented thanks to the combination of environments on site that have led community members like Jessica Kagle, the director of Kestrel, to push for the property to become a nature learning center.

"The vision is to have a space with a big open classroom that has displays highlighting the special wetland and forest wildlife, and value of the property with the constellation of really sensitive habitats that are here," Kagle said. "I would really like to see routine, accessible public programming several times a week."

The nature learning center proposal would not include any new buildings or structures, due to the conservation restriction on the property. Instead, the proposal focuses on utilizing the existing building for a small office space, a potential space for raising endangered turtle hatchlings, student work displays, and an expansion of the gear-loaning library where visitors could borrow equipment such nets, boots, and local field guides to explore the surrounding wetlands.

With Kestrel already equipped with a staff of expert naturalists who have been focused on teaching wetlands ecology to Beverly for the past 22 years, the proposal aims to incur no cost to the city by utilizing a variety grant fundings and Kestrel's preexisting staff.

Justin Freedman, a parent and direct abutter to Camp Paradise, said that from his own observations the space is underutilized, with the main building often being locked and inaccessible to the public.

"My kids and I love the outdoors and feel lucky to have such a special place to experience nature and have fun outdoors," Freedman said. "Unfortunately, this site is underutilized and often seems neglected. My kids and I frequently clean up trash that is dumped there and the building is always locked and is in need of maintenance.

"The possibility of it being used as a nature learning center at no additional cost to the town seems like an ideal use of the facility for all of the public to enjoy."

Due to the land being protected under Article 97 of state law, the city has thus far been unwilling to consider proposals by Kagle for the creation of the nature learning center, with Mayor Mike Cahill saying the proposal would require a disposition of the land.

Under Article 97 and the terms of the Parkland Acquisitions and Renovations for Communities (PARC) grant awarded by the state for the city to purchase the property, disposition is prohibited without the city first obtaining, among other things, a two-thirds roll call vote of each house of the Legislature, approval from Secretary of EEA, and acquiring or dedicating replacement land.

"The land is protected by Article 97 of the Constitution of the Commonwealth and the priority remains the needs of the city," Cahill said in a statement. "At this time, the city is satisfied with the current programming and is not interested in changing the use of the space. A use of the land that could be interpreted as a lease of the land could be considered a disposition."

In response to this statement, Kagle emphasized that Kestrel is not looking for a transfer of ownership of Camp Paradise or a lease. Instead, the proposal is for a partnership in which the city grants Kestrel a renewable license for up to a year for a purpose consistent with conservation.

"We are proposing a partnership where we work with the city, make some suggestions, listen to their goals, take input from the general public and provide a service," Kagle said. "We're not interested in anything that would challenge the existing protections. Article 97 is not triggered by having a nature center operated by a nonprofit. It is only triggered by changes in use to non-conservation related uses, or changes to structures."

Today, Camp Paradise is used by organizations like Beverly's Girl Scout Troop 4, Kestrel, and the city's Parks and Recreation Department. The Recreation Department runs occasional programs throughout the year, including a class on identifying and foraging local plants last July, a six-week beginner oil painting class on Saturdays during the winter, as well as a "Polar Park" February vacation program for kids with games, arts and crafts, and outdoor recreation.

Kagle said Kestrel would continue to share the property with any other city or local organizations looking to utilize the space for compatible uses. Kagle also indicated they would offer support in the form of naturalist services and equipment loans to enhance the usage of the Girl Scouts, who have a guaranteed right to a certain amount of site usage as part of the original sale documents.

"We envision Kestrel caring for and programming the site, while collaborating to share it with others in the community," Kagle said. "We have no interest in restrictive or exclusive use of Camp Paradise. We envision more, not less, use by the community at large, including groups such as the Scouts."

The issuance of a revocable permit or license of limited duration is not considered to be a disposition of land subject to Article 97, as long as it doesn't transfer any interest in land or authorize a change in how the land is used, According to the state Executive Office of Environmental Affairs.

Kagle cited other nature learning centers in Massachusetts that have been established on Article 97 land, including at Cambridge's Magazine Beach, where in 2021 the state Department of Conservation and Recreation awarded Mass Audubon, a private nonprofit, with a five-year license to the park's historic powder house to transform it into a three-season facility with free drop-in nature programs.

"Beverly is one of the few towns in Essex County that doesn't have a major natural resource center, and I think we're really well positioned to have one," Kagle said. "As the only building on wild public land in Beverly, I think it's important to use the Camp Paradise lodge in a way that is directly related to the precious wild land it is situated upon.

"Wetlands require wildlife corridors, safe crossings between wetlands on migration nights, siltation fences, and a lot of other additional work to actually conserve them — and that can't happen without public awareness."

All trees, branches, and shrubs, hedges, bushes, and other vegetation located upon any public way or upon any private premises adjacent to the public way shall be trimmed so that the lowest projecting branches provide a clearance height of not less than 14 feet above the travel portion of a public street and not less than eight feet above the public sidewalk.

1. The City Arborist may waive the provisions of this section for newly planted or naturally low-profile trees if he/she determines that they do not interfere with public travel, obstruct the light of any streetlight, obstruct the view of any traffic sign or signal, or endanger public safety.

2. The Director of Municipal Inspections or their designee shall enforce the provisions of this section. Violations of the provisions of this section shall be a warning for the first offense and a fine of $100 for the second or subsequent offenses, with each day of violation constituting a separate offense.

3. In addition to fines for violation of this section, the Department of Public Services or its designee is authorized to trim or prune any interfering or obstructing tree, branch, shrub, hedge, bush, and other vegetation upon any private premises back to the private property lot line. In such an event, the property owner shall be liable for the cost to the City of eliminating the interference or obstruction. Any fee not paid within 60 days of the demand shall become, upon application of the Treasurer-Collector of the City of the Beverly, a lien upon the property.

### § 15-37 Human Rights Committee.

[Added 10-19-2015 by Ord. No. 453; amended 5-20-2024 by Ord. No. 101A; 9-23-2024 by Ord. No. 101B]

A. Establishment; composition.

(1) There is hereby established a Human Rights Committee. This Committee shall consist of 11 members. The Committee shall ~~also~~ include one member from the City administration and one member from the School Department. Members of the Committee serve without compensation and shall be appointed by the Mayor, subject to confirmation by the City Council, for a term of three years and a maximum term limit of six consecutive years; provided, however, that an individual who has served for six consecutive years may be appointed to the Committee again after at least one year of not serving on the Committee.

(2) The membership shall, so far as practicable, be so selected as to provide broad representation from the community, including but not limited to individuals with experience, either lived or learned, in advocating for civil and human rights, business, education, immigration, labor, law, law enforcement, public health, and religion.

(3) Committee members who are appointed by virtue of their status as a City or a school employee shall not be required to be residents. Committee members shall not be required to be registered voters of the City. Up to two members may be under the age of 18, as long as they are at least 16 years old.

(4) A quorum of the Committee shall be a majority of the members serving on the Committee, so long as there are no fewer than seven (7) members serving on the Committee at that time.
